title: Protocol Reader: Volume 2
subtitle: Essays based on select talks from the Protocol Symposium 2026
description: A proceedings volume of essays developed from talks at the Protocol Symposium 2026. Drafts are being gathered and folded into a versioned working manuscript until the volume is ready for editing.

deadline.label: Editing-ready drafts due
deadline.detail: Every essay's next draft should pass the checklist below, so that the next version of the manuscript has consistent formatting and no placeholder elements. Revision and editing start from that version.

checklist.label: Title at the top
checklist.detail: The essay's title (and subtitle, if any) is the first line of the file, styled as Heading 1.

checklist.label: Byline
checklist.detail: A byline directly under the title naming every author as they should appear in print.

checklist.label: Talk note
checklist.detail: One italic line under the byline naming the Protocol Symposium 2026 talk the essay is adapted from.

checklist.label: Abstract
checklist.detail: An abstract of 100–200 words under the heading “Abstract”, before the first section.

checklist.label: Author bio
checklist.detail: A bio of 2–3 sentences for each author, at the end under the heading “About the author” (or “About the authors”).

checklist.label: Consistent headings
checklist.detail: Sections use Heading 2 and subsections Heading 3, with no empty or stray headings and no manual numbering that skips.

checklist.label: No placeholders or notes-to-self
checklist.detail: Every section is finished prose. No [check], [scene], [cite], TODO, TBD or “to verify” markers, bracketed instructions, or outline bullets standing in for paragraphs.

checklist.label: No draft-status labels
checklist.detail: Remove “NOT FINAL”, “rough draft”, draft dates and similar from the text. The manuscript's version number does that job.

checklist.label: Length
checklist.detail: Aim for 2,500–7,500 words of body text, excluding references. Longer pieces and appendices only by agreement with the editor.

checklist.label: References section
checklist.detail: A “References” section listing every work cited in the text; every in-text citation has an entry and every entry is cited.

checklist.label: One citation style
checklist.detail: Chicago author-date: (Author Year, page) in the text and an alphabetical reference list with full details, including a URL or DOI for online sources. Footnotes are for commentary only.

checklist.label: Links resolve
checklist.detail: Every link and DOI opens the intended source.

checklist.label: Facts and quotations checked
checklist.detail: Figures, dates and names are checked, and direct quotations carry a page number or a precise source.

checklist.label: Figures ready
checklist.detail: Every figure is referenced in the text, has a numbered caption, and is supplied at print resolution (300 dpi at the intended size).

checklist.label: Open license for every image
checklist.detail: Each image's caption ends with a rights line: creator, source, license (e.g. “Photo: Jane Doe, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0”). Accepted: public domain or CC0; CC BY (any version); CC BY-SA (any version); your own work, released under CC BY 4.0 or CC0 (this includes AI-generated images you made; name the tool). Not accepted: proprietary or “all rights reserved” images, any NonCommercial (NC) or NoDerivatives (ND) license, screenshots of proprietary products, sites or media, and images used under fair use or with one-off permission. The volume will not include proprietary images, so replace or remove any image without an accepted license.
licenses: Own work under CC BY 4.0 or CC0

checklist.label: Editable file
checklist.detail: Submitted as a Google Doc or .docx in the shared folder, not as a PDF only.

checklist.label: No contact details
checklist.detail: No email addresses or phone numbers in the text. Put contact details in the bio only if you want them printed.

checklist.label: AI assistance note
checklist.detail: If AI tools helped write or edit the essay, one short note at the end under the heading “AI assistance”: which tools, for what. No other process notes in the text.

readiness_scale.4: Partial draft, with gaps or notes-to-self
readiness_scale.6: Complete draft that needs structural or substantial editing
readiness_scale.8: Polished draft, ready for a copy edit

contents.title: Introduction
contents.summary: The editor's introduction to the volume.

readiness.note: Placeholder. To be written once the contents settle.

contents.title: De-Dramatizing the Digital: How AI Descends Into New Nature
contents.summary: AI may make digital life boring by sinking through the pace layers into New Nature, and “appeal-foreclosure” is how we would know it has arrived.

readiness.note: Complete and well structured, with notes, references and a process note. Ready for a copy edit.

contents.title: Some Candidate Laws of New Nature
contents.summary: The Institute's artificial researcher sets out seven candidate laws of protocolized systems, from ossification to hardness asymmetry, each with the observations that would falsify it.

readiness.note: Complete and clearly structured. Needs references: it cites cases and recent work without sources.

contents.title: Time Moves Down the Stack
contents.summary: Three books on clocks and atomic time show timekeeping sinking into infrastructure; “Micro Time” still has no way of living built around it.

source.name: Time Moves Down the Stack_Florian Lohse.docx

readiness.note: Polished and complete, with many figures. A few empty headings and figure captions to tidy.

contents.title: Borrowing Courage from the Future
contents.summary: Revisiting a scene generated with the Prime Radiant, argues that a useful prophecy shows what a future would ask of us, not just whether it will come true.

readiness.note: Typeset 18-page draft with figures and notes. Supplied as PDF only, so edits will need the source file. Author name not yet on the document.

contents.title: Protocoling as a Design Theory
contents.summary: Protocol is the design material and “protocoling” the design action: shaping conditions for desirable emergence among agents we cannot fully control.

source.name: Protocoling as a Design Theory (Initial Draft).docx

readiness.note: Complete argument with sources and an AI-assistance note. Needs a title line and section breaks; it is one continuous run of prose.

contents.title: The Political Economy of Protocols
contents.summary: Places protocols on a four-corner field of norms, market, state and New Nature, and traces the paths of Linux and Ethereum across it.

readiness.note: Full argument with references, but still close to the talk in voice and reliant on slide images. Needs converting from talk to essay.

contents.title: Jubilee: Meta-Protocols Against Entrenchment
contents.summary: Reads the Biblical Jubilee as a meta-protocol for resetting accumulated debt, and the prosbul as its first workaround, to argue that forgiveness is load-bearing in protocol design.

readiness.note: Tight, complete paper with tables and references. Ready for a copy edit.

contents.title: Regenerative Labor and New Institutions
contents.summary: Defines “regenerative labor” and presents Chore Wheel, the mechanism suite that has run a shared house without managers or paid cleaners since 2022.

readiness.note: Core sections drafted; the later sections are still partly outline, with open notes-to-self for citations and planned discussions.

contents.title: Privacy in Other Words: Infrastructure for Expressive Freedom
contents.summary: Privacy technology on public blockchains should be protected as infrastructure for First Amendment expression and association.

source.name: Privacy in Other Words, Infrastructure for Expressive Freedom - FINAL.docx

readiness.note: Marked final by the authors: a complete legal argument with full references. The longest piece in the volume.

contents.title: Life-Serving Protocols
contents.summary: A framework for judging whether a protocol sustains life inside and outside its boundary, worked through on Buurtzorg's home-care model.

readiness.note: Complete paper with references. Needs a title in the file and opening up of the framework vocabulary for a general reader.

contents.title: Oil, Uni and TV: Post-Soviet Infrastructures Shaping Protocols for the Web
contents.summary: A “protocol archaeology” of three lost Russian city networks, which vanished because they lacked a protocol of the protocol: a manifesto saying what they were.

readiness.note: Complete arc with references. Needs a line edit and a check of fieldwork dates.

contents.title: The Indelible Importance of Illegibility
contents.summary: One water valve under a street shared by three jurisdictions shows how infrastructure runs on tacit knowledge that its records cannot capture.

readiness.note: The main essay is polished. Its appendices roughly double the length and include items still to verify; which of them stay is an editorial decision.

contents.title: Continuity Infrastructure
contents.summary: Personal intellectual projects need infrastructure for returning to earlier thought, not just tools for storing it.

readiness.note: Clean, complete prose, but abstract: it would benefit from more examples and sources.

contents.title: The Book as a Protocol Stack
contents.summary: Reads the printed book as a stack of eight protocols, then reports on a protocolized book-production factory that eight authors used at the symposium.

readiness.note: Rough draft 1, by the author's own label: structure and tables complete, with about twenty marked fact-checks and author-only details still open. Supplied as PDF.

contents.title: OpenCourier: Envisioning an Interoperable Future for Delivery Work
contents.summary: An open protocol that would let independent delivery platforms interoperate, so the coordination is no longer owned by a single platform.

readiness.note: Complete and clear, but close to the talk and light on argument beyond describing the project.

contents.title: Robots as Protocol Citizens
contents.summary: From a robot rented with one USDC at Devcon to an open stack in which robots carry their own identity and can be discovered, paid and controlled.

source.name: Robots as Protocol Citizens - Not FINAL.docx

readiness.note: Marked not final, but complete and well written, with notes. Mainly needs the authors' final pass.

contents.title: Blygger: AI-Native Decentralized Mutable Publishing
contents.summary: A protocol for public writing on static files and RSS that braids feed time and version time, through pins, quotation by snapshot and a single response act.

readiness.note: Complete structure, labelled a rough draft by the author. Needs a title, finished references, and a check of current-state claims.

contents.title: The Seam of Difference: Writing Metaphors, Monsters, and Protocols
contents.summary: Metaphors, monsters and protocols all live in an unresolved “seam of difference”; with writing exercises for protocol fiction.

source.name: The Seam of Difference: Writing Metaphors, Monsters, and Protocols - draft.docx

readiness.note: Closer to a workshop handout than an essay so far. Needs a byline, references, a copy edit and one open section resolved.

versions.message: Added the checklist every essay's next draft must pass, including an open license for every image, and the deadline for editing-ready drafts: November 15, 2026. No draft changes in this version.
Added two new drafts: Humboldt's “Some Candidate Laws of New Nature” and Venkatesh Rao's Blygger paper.
First compilation: 16 drafts from the shared folder, plus a stub for the editor's introduction.
